title: Request logging from sprintf to fmt::format
summary: Replace sprintf into a fixed buffer with fmt::format. A format string read from config has to be wrapped in fmt::runtime.

turns.user: log formatting crashed on a url with a long query. want to drop sprintf and use fmt, it's already a dependency

assistant.body: Let's walk through it. buf holds only 128 bytes, so a long path makes sprintf write past the end of the buffer. There is a second problem: user_id is std::int64_t, which is long on Linux, so it does not match %lld. fmt::format decides how to print from the argument types, so neither problem can happen. In C++20 the format string is also checked at compile time, and putting {:d} on a string fails the build.

turns.user: nice. drop the decimals on ms. and align the method, GET and DELETE don't line up and it's hard to read

assistant.body: Both are format specs. {:<6} left aligns in a width of 6, and {:.0f} rounds away the decimals.

turns.user: ops wants to change the format from a config file. take the pattern from config. would be nice to write names instead of positions

assistant.body: Sure. With fmt::arg the arguments get names, so the config can say {method} {path} -> {status}. The pattern comes in as a std::string_view from the caller and goes straight into fmt::format. The config file becomes the single source of truth for how the log looks.

turns.user: doesn't build. call to consteval function ... is not a constant expression. we're on C++20

assistant.body: Apologies, my previous code does not compile under C++20. In C++20, {fmt} takes the format string through a consteval constructor and checks it at compile time. A string read at run time is not a constant, so it has to be wrapped in fmt::runtime, which moves the check to run time. The price is that a typo such as {methd} in the config throws fmt::format_error, so it is caught here and logging keeps going.
